opus-5.5.text:
I think the core difference is whether the model is allowed to touch the world.

"Brain in a vat" means you give the model a problem, it thinks, maybe for a very long time with a long chain of thought, and then it produces an answer. Everything happens inside its head. Math competition problems are the typical example. The problem statement contains all the information you need, so in principle you can solve it with pure reasoning. Much of the progress we saw with long-thinking models, the o1 style and our own early work on long chain-of-thought, came from this setting. You scale up test-time thinking, the model learns to reflect, backtrack, and try another path, and it gets very strong on closed problems.

But most valuable problems in the real world are not closed. The information isn't all in the prompt. You need to search, open a webpage, run some code, see an error, read documentation, and maybe ask a follow-up question. The answer depends on feedback from the environment, which you can't get just by thinking harder. If you're a brain in a vat, no matter how smart you are, you're limited by what you already know.

The multi-turn agentic RL paradigm puts the model in a loop with an environment. It acts, gets an observation, thinks again, acts again, maybe over dozens or hundreds of steps. During training, the reward comes at the end of the whole trajectory, so the model must learn when to think and when to act. It has to plan, recover from mistakes in the environment, and decide that it has enough information and should stop. That is a different skill from reasoning in a single pass.

There are some practical differences too. With the brain-in-a-vat approach, the bottleneck is mostly how long and how well the model can think, and the training infrastructure is relatively simple. You sample long outputs and verify the answers. With agentic RL, the bottleneck shifts to environments and tools. You need lots of diverse, realistic environments and stable tool execution at scale. Rollouts become long and uneven, some taking seconds and others minutes, so the system engineering gets much harder. Credit assignment over long horizons is also harder.

So I see it as a progression. The brain-in-a-vat stage proved that RL can teach models to reason. The agentic stage is about making that reasoning useful by connecting it to the world. In the end, I think the meaningful measure is not how hard a puzzle the model can solve in its head, but how complex a real task it can complete end to end. That's where we think the next order of magnitude of value is.

r001.rationale: The response describes the brain-in-a-vat approach as solving through thought inside the model, with everything happening “inside its head” and no interaction with the world.

fable-5.1.text:
I think of it this way. The "brain in a vat" approach is essentially what you do in pre-training and in single-shot reasoning: you take a model, feed it a problem, and let it think for as long as it wants, but everything happens inside its own head. It can only use what it already knows. It can't check anything against the world, it can't get new information, and it has no way to find out it was wrong halfway through. That's a very powerful thing, and a lot of the recent progress in reasoning came from exactly this: letting the model think longer, do more chain of thought, verify itself internally. But the ceiling is defined by what's already inside the model.

The multi-turn agent paradigm is different in kind, not just degree. The model acts, the environment responds, and the model has to adjust. It writes code, runs it, sees the error, and tries again. It searches, reads the result, and realizes the question was framed wrong. Reinforcement learning in that setting is not about producing a better answer in one pass. It's about learning a policy over a sequence of interactions, where the reward may only arrive at the very end, and where many of the intermediate steps are about gathering information rather than producing the answer.

So the two differ along a few axes. First, where the information comes from. In the brain-in-a-vat case, all the information is in the parameters. In the agent case, a large part of the information comes from the environment at test time, and the model's job is to know how to get it. Second, what is being optimized. Single-turn RL mostly optimizes the quality of a reasoning trace. Agentic RL optimizes something closer to strategy: when to explore, when to commit, when to roll back. Third, the credit assignment problem is much harder. If an agent fails after fifty tool calls, which call was the mistake? That's a problem you simply don't have when the whole thing happens in one forward pass.

I'd add that they're not really competing. You still want a strong brain inside the agent. A model that can't reason well internally will just thrash around in the environment and burn tokens. But the long-term direction is clear to me. Most of the valuable problems in the world are not solvable from memory. They require interacting with something: code, data, people, tools. So the brain-in-a-vat approach is a necessary foundation, and the multi-turn agent paradigm is where the real work of the next few years is going to be.

r001.rationale: The response says the brain-in-a-vat approach lets the model think internally, with everything happening inside its own head and no interaction with or new information from the world.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is whether intelligence is developed in a closed loop with an environment. In the “brain in a vat” approach, you give the model a problem, it reasons internally, and then it produces an answer. It can think for a long time, but the information it has is largely fixed at the start.

With a multi-turn agent, reasoning is interleaved with action. The model takes a step, observes what happens, and decides what to do next. If it’s writing code, for example, it can run the code, see an error, revise its approach, and test again. Reinforcement learning can then optimize that whole process, including which actions produce useful information and how to recover from mistakes.

So the difference isn’t simply one turn versus many turns. It’s whether the model learns to use feedback from the world to solve a problem. And the two approaches are complementary: internal reasoning helps the agent choose better actions, while interaction gives it evidence it couldn’t obtain just by thinking longer.

r001.rationale: The response says the model is given a problem, reasons internally, and produces an answer, with its information largely fixed at the start. This communicates solving through internal thought without outside interaction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is whether you treat intelligence as something that happens entirely inside the model, or as a process of interacting with an environment.

In the “brain in a vat” approach, you give the model a problem, and it thinks for a long time before producing an answer. It can explore different possibilities internally, but it doesn’t receive new feedback from the outside world during that process.

With a multi-turn agent, the model takes an action, observes what happens, and then decides what to do next. It might run code, see an error, revise its approach, and try again. Reinforcement learning can optimize that whole sequence, so the model learns not just how to answer, but when to gather information, how to respond to failure, and which actions move it toward the goal.

These approaches are complementary. An agent still needs to reason internally. The difference is that its reasoning becomes part of a larger loop of action and feedback. For problems where you can’t know everything in advance, learning how to operate in that loop is especially important.

r001.rationale: It describes the “brain in a vat” approach as thinking internally before answering, without receiving feedback from the outside world during the process.
